speaker: jasonwandner
text: Your Honors. My name is Jason Wander. I'm Appellant Counsel for Ishmael Peters. Your Honors, may it please the Court. Mr. Corrente, good morning, sir. A trial lawyer in a criminal case, Your Honors, has three basic functions. One is to know the record and know the facts and know the law of the case. The next is to confront the prosecution's case. And thirdly is to present the defendant's case. In the trial of Ishmael Peters, the trial lawyer swung and missed each one of those instances. Ishmael Peters struck out when the lawyer swung and missed three times and he was convicted and sentenced to life in prison. This was a case where there was no forensic evidence. There was no DNA evidence. There was utterly no corroboration whatsoever. The entire case rested on the sworn testimony of multiple witnesses, convicted felons, all who had motivations to lie, motivations to have somebody else take the fall to help themselves. The trial lawyer failed in his job to confront those witnesses and impeach those witnesses, destroying their credibility and the credibility of the state's case with evidence that he had. In some instances, he knew he had it. In some instances, he didn't even know he had it. Either way, he was unable to introduce it in a manner that would be in any way competent. And we take no issue when we agree with the trial lawyer, excuse me, with the post-conviction court's ruling that the trial lawyer was in fact incompetent. What we take issue with in this appeal is his conclusion that those deficiencies did not prejudice the defendant. That conclusion was erroneous. The case law is clear. In a case where there is little or no corroboration, like here, the defense must impeach the credibility of the witnesses. In this case, that was not done. Had the lawyer adequately used the evidence he had, for instance, the evidence that even this court in its ruling on the direct appeal found to be compelling enough to indicate that there was no prejudice for the defendant to bring before the post-conviction court, the issue of Denae Craig.
